props.title: Hour of the Gun
props.initialSlug: Revenge and justice collide in Wyatt Earp's West

sections.content: **Hour of the Gun** (1967) marks a fascinating shift in how Westerns portrayed the Wyatt Earp legend, stripping away mythmaking to show a darker, more morally ambiguous take. Unlike John Ford's romanticized **My Darling Clementine** (1946), director John Sturges crafts a psychological Western focused on revenge and corruption. James Garner's cold, vengeful Earp is worlds away from the noble lawman played by Henry Fonda - this Earp becomes increasingly brutal in his pursuit of justice after the OK Corral shootout.

sections.content: The late 1960s marked a crucial transition in Western filmmaking, with films like **Hour of the Gun** and **The Wild Bunch** (1969) deconstructing genre myths. These revisionist Westerns questioned the traditional hero narrative, showing lawmen and outlaws as complex, flawed figures operating in a morally gray frontier. Sturges, who previously directed **The Magnificent Seven** (1960), brings a measured, almost documentary-like approach to the violence, making it feel consequential rather than glorified.

James Garner's performance as Earp represents a significant departure from his usual affable screen persona. His portrayal aligns with other morally compromised Western protagonists of the era, like Paul Newman's title character in **Hombre** (1967) and Clint Eastwood's William Munny in **Unforgiven** (1992). The film's focus on the aftermath of the OK Corral shootout, rather than building up to it, allows for a deeper exploration of vengeance's psychological toll. sections.content: **Hour of the Gun** bridges the gap between classic Western heroism and the genre's darker modern iterations. Its influence can be seen in later works like **Open Range** (2003) and **3:10 to Yuma** (2007), which similarly explore the complex motivations of their protagonists. The film's attention to historical detail and psychological realism helped pave the way for more nuanced Western storytelling.
